newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo '97 trade gap may exceed $2 bln - institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugo '97 trade gap may exceed $2 bln - institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's trade gap may exceed two billion dollars this year if stagnation of exports and slowdown of imports continues at the present pace, the Belgrade-based Foreign Trade Institute said on Tuesday.
"Imports slow down and stagnation of exports characterises foreign trade in the first five months of the year," said the institute's director Radovan Kovacevic.
"If such tendencies continue, the trade deficit could again be well above two billion dollars this year," he told a news conference.
Exports have been stagnating since last June and their monthly value has not exceeded $200 million since then, Kovacevic said.
On the other hand there was a slowdown in imports due to limited funds to finance them, he said.
Despite these tendencies, the trade deficit in January-Mayreached $847 million, with exports worth $862 million and imports $1.709 billion.
According to Kovacevic, a dramatic increase of exports was unlikely in the short run due to an unfavourable foreign trade structure.
"The structure of domestic industries and products has not changed compared to last year," he said.
Raw materials and semi-finished goods account for $1.179 billion, consumer goods $327 million and investment products $203 million of total five months imports.

Top of the list of exports were non-ferrous metals at the value of $119.5 million, iron and steel ($88.3 million), fruit and vegetables ($42.4 million), tobacco and tobacco products ($41 million), plastic materials in primary form ($36.4 million) and textiles ($27.7 million).
In 1996 , Yugoslavia recorded a trade gap of $2.26 billion, with exports worth $1.84 billion and imports $4.1 billion.
The government's plan for 1997 was to keep the deficit close to $2 billion by boosting exports by 48 percent and imports by 20 percent. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
